summary: This standards-track document defines CBOR Web Token, a compact way to represent claims transferred between two parties. The claims are encoded in CBOR and protected with COSE for application-layer security. It is like JWT, but suited to constrained environments.

plainLanguage.summary: A CBOR Web Token carries the same kind of signed statements about a user that a JSON Web Token does, but written in a compact binary form. That suits small, battery-powered devices that spend energy on every byte sent.

subtitle: A compact, binary token for constrained devices, using CBOR claims protected by COSE instead of JSON.

tldr.problem: JSON Web Tokens are widely used, but JSON encoding is considered inefficient for some Internet of Things systems that use low-power radio technologies, where every byte of a message costs power.
tldr.mechanism: CWT keeps the JWT claim names and rules but encodes the claims in CBOR, whose map keys can be integers. Protection uses COSE, which can sign, MAC or encrypt the token.
tldr.outcome: A token that carries the same seven registered claims as a JWT in a smaller binary form, with a registered CBOR tag, a media type and a CoAP content format. The RFC is a Proposed Standard from May 2018 and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Registered claims
facts.value: iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, cti

today: RFC 8392 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2018. It has not been obsoleted and nothing in the unit metadata updates it, so it remains the definition of the CBOR Web Token, with COSE in RFC 8152 providing the protection and CBOR in RFC 7049 providing the encoding.

sections.title: A Smaller Token
sections.content:
The JSON Web Token (JWT) is a standardized security token format that has found use in OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect deployments, among other applications. JWT uses JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Encryption to secure the contents of the JWT, which is a set of claims represented in JSON.

The use of JSON for encoding information is popular for Web and native applications, but it is considered inefficient for some Internet of Things systems that use low-power radio technologies. RFC 8392 defines an alternative encoding of claims. Instead of JSON it uses CBOR, and calls the result CBOR Web Token (CWT), a compact means of representing secured claims to be transferred between two parties.

CWT is closely related to JWT. It references the JWT claims, and both its name and its pronunciation are derived from JWT; the suggested pronunciation of CWT is the same as the English word "cot". To protect the claims, the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) specification is used.
sections.plainLanguage: JSON is easy to read but wasteful on a tiny radio. CWT writes the same statements in a compact binary form that a small device can send without spending much power.

sections.title: How CBOR Maps Differ
sections.content:
In JSON, maps are called objects and have only one kind of map key: a string. CBOR uses strings, negative integers and unsigned integers as map keys. The integers are used for compactness of encoding and easy comparison, and the inclusion of strings allows for an additional range of short encoded values to be used.

A claim is a piece of information asserted about a subject, represented as a name and value pair. In CWT terms, the Claim Name is the human-readable name that identifies a claim, the Claim Key is the CBOR map key that identifies it, and the Claim Value is the CBOR map value holding the value. The CWT Claims Set is the CBOR map that contains the claims conveyed by the CWT.

Two types are reused from JWT with a different encoding. StringOrURI is represented as a CBOR text string instead of a JSON text string. NumericDate is represented as a CBOR numeric date, with the modification that the leading tag 1 for an epoch-based date and time MUST be omitted.
sections.plainLanguage: In CBOR a map can be numbered, so a claim can be called 1 instead of "iss". That saves space, and it means a reader can compare keys without decoding strings.

sections.title: The Registered Claims
sections.content:
Which claims a CWT must contain to be valid depends on the context and is outside the scope of the specification. In the absence of application-specific requirements, all claims that are not understood by implementations MUST be ignored.

The RFC registers seven claims, none of which is intended to be mandatory to use or implement. They provide a starting point for a set of useful, interoperable claims, and applications should define which specific claims they use and when they are required or optional. Each is the same claim as in JWT, with one difference in how the value is written.

The iss issuer claim uses Claim Key 1 and carries a text string. The sub subject claim uses Claim Key 2 and carries a text string. The aud audience claim uses Claim Key 3 and carries a text string, or an array whose elements are text strings. The exp expiration time claim uses Claim Key 4 and the nbf not before claim uses Claim Key 5, each carrying an integer or floating-point number. The iat issued at claim uses Claim Key 6 and carries an integer or floating-point number. The cti CWT ID claim uses Claim Key 7 and carries a byte string.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven claims are registered, each with a small number in place of its name. Who issued the token, who it is about, who it is for, when it expires, when it starts, when it was issued, and a unique identifier.

sections.title: Tags on Claims and on Tokens
sections.content:
The claim values defined in this specification MUST NOT be prefixed with any CBOR tag. While CBOR tag 1 for an epoch-based date and time could logically be prefixed to the values of the exp, nbf and iat claims, this is unnecessary, since the representation of the claim values is already specified by the claim definitions. Tagging claim values would only take up extra space without adding information. This does not prohibit future claim definitions from requiring tags for specific claims.

How to determine that a CBOR data structure is a CWT is application dependent. In some cases the information is known from the application context, such as the position of the CWT in a data structure where the value must be a CWT. One method is to use the application/cwt content type in the transport protocol.

As another means for applications to declare that a CBOR data structure is a CWT, the RFC defines the CWT CBOR tag. Its use is optional and is intended for cases where this information would not otherwise be known. If present, the CWT tag MUST prefix a tagged object using one of the COSE CBOR tags, for example the COSE_Mac0 tag, whose value is 17.
sections.plainLanguage: Claim values carry no extra labels, because the claim definition already says what they are. The token as a whole can carry a tag with the number 61 so a reader can tell it is a CWT without outside help.

sections.title: Creating and Validating a CWT
sections.content:
To create a CWT, the creator builds a CWT Claims Set with the desired claims, and lets the Message be the binary representation of that set. It creates a COSE Header holding the desired header parameters, which MUST be valid per the COSE specification. Then it protects the Message in one of three ways: as a COSE_Sign or COSE_Sign1 object when the CWT is signed, as a COSE_Mac or COSE_Mac0 object when it is MACed, or as a COSE_Encrypt or COSE_Encrypt0 object when it is encrypted. If a nested operation is to be performed, the Message becomes the tagged COSE object and the process starts again. Finally the application may prepend the COSE CBOR tag, and then the CWT CBOR tag.

To validate a CWT, the validator first checks that it is a valid CBOR object. If it begins with the CWT CBOR tag, that tag is removed and one of the COSE CBOR tags must follow; that COSE tag is removed and used to determine the type of the CWT. If there is no COSE tag, the type comes from the application context. The validator checks that the COSE Header includes only parameters and values whose syntax and semantics are both understood and supported, or that are specified as being ignored when not understood.

The validator then follows the COSE steps for signing, MAC or encryption objects, and lets the Message be the payload or the resulting plaintext. If the Message begins with a COSE CBOR tag, the token was the subject of nested operations and validation starts again with that Message. Finally the Message must be a valid CBOR map, and that map is the CWT Claims Set. If any of the steps fail, the CWT MUST be rejected and treated by the application as invalid input.
sections.plainLanguage: Building a token means filling in the claims and then signing, MACing or encrypting them with COSE. Checking one means undoing that and then confirming the claims are a proper map. Any failed step means the token is rejected.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of a CWT relies on the protections offered by COSE. Unless the claims in a CWT are protected, an adversary can modify, add or remove claims.

Since the claims conveyed in a CWT may be used to make authorization decisions, it is not only important to protect the CWT in transit but also to ensure that the recipient can authenticate the party that assembled the claims and created the CWT. Without trust in the recipient of the party that created the CWT, no sensible authorization decision can be made. The creator of the CWT also needs to evaluate each claim value carefully before including it, so the recipient can be assured of the validity of the information provided.

Syntactically, the signing and encryption operations for nested CWTs may be applied in any order. However, if both signing and encryption are necessary, producers normally should sign the message and then encrypt the result, thus encrypting the signature. This prevents attacks in which the signature is stripped, leaving just an encrypted message, and it provides privacy for the signer. Signatures over encrypted text are also not considered valid in many jurisdictions.
sections.plainLanguage: An unprotected token can be edited by anyone in the middle. The receiver must also know who built the token before trusting what it says. When a token is both signed and encrypted, sign first and encrypt the signature, so that the signature cannot be quietly removed.

sections.title: Registered Names and Numbers
sections.content:
Several registries carry entries for CWT. The "CBOR Web Token (CWT) Claims" registry holds the claim names and keys. Registration requests are reviewed by Designated Experts over a three-week review period on a mailing list, and values in the limited set between -256 and 255, and strings of length 1, are restricted to claims with general applicability. The registration template sets out the ranges: integer values from -256 to 255 and strings of length 1 are designated as Standards Action; integer values from -65536 to -257 and from 256 to 65535, along with strings of length 2, are Specification Required; integers greater than 65535 and strings longer than 2 are Expert Review; and integers less than -65536 are Private Use. Key 0 is reserved by the initial registry contents.

The media type application/cwt is registered in the Media Types registry, with encoding considerations of binary and intended usage of COMMON. It is used by IoT applications sending security tokens over HTTP(S), CoAP(S) and other transports. The CoAP content-format ID for that media type is 61, and the CBOR tag registered for a CWT is also 61.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbers were set aside so that programs can recognise a CWT. The media type is application/cwt, and both the CBOR tag and the CoAP content format use the number 61.
